question: For decades, over 220 000 barrels of radioactive waste were dumped in the Atlantic, with some of the dumping sites located just 630 kilometres from Galicia.

The NODSSUM project has just finished assessing the state of these barrels, and the results have caused significant concern in my community; researchers have confirmed that several of the barrels inspected are in an advanced state of deterioration and have also detected radionuclides characteristic of this waste at higher concentrations than expected in the surrounding area. In light of the above: 1.
Given the transboundary nature of the environmental risks at play, will the Commission take appropriate measures to ensure that the Member States concerned thoroughly monitor the affected area?

Should the Commission ask those in charge of the NODSSUM project to make the scientific data obtained during the observation missions available to it, will it do so and will it actively participate in activities to verify the state of the radioactive waste by coordinating a response at European level, based on the most up-to-date scientific knowledge?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.10.2026) In line with the Commission’s previous replies1, the Commission has no mandate for dealing with radioactivity in international waters but is closely monitoring the situation.

Pursuant to Article 35 of the Euratom Treaty, the Commission is however entitled to verify the operation and efficiency of Member States’ facilities necessary to carry out continuous monitoring of the level of radioactivity in the air, water and soil2. The Commission has verified the adequacy of radioactivity monitoring facilities located on Euratom Community territory, i.e.

, in the Galicia and Cantabrian coastal marine environment, which showed that the facilities necessary for the monitoring of levels of radioactivity were adequate3. The Commission is aware of the preliminary findings of the NODSSUM mission4 and follows the NODSSUM project in established international expert fora, e.g., in OSPAR’s Radioactive Substance Committee5.
